documents.unit: Office of Academic Affairs & Provost (AI at Tulane site)
documents.title: Artificial Intelligence at Tulane University: Guidelines for the Ethical and Responsible Use of AI
documents.stance_why: The page says students' AI use is 'already covered in our academic integrity policies', that faculty should 'explore' AI 'rather than restricting' it, and that 'each instructor has the option of putting in place guidelines' for their course. It sets no university-wide rule on student AI use and hands the decision to instructors, so delegates.
documents.summary: Provost-linked AI site with institutional investment notes plus guidelines on transparency, data protection and tool review. It points student AI use to academic integrity policies, lets each instructor set course rules, and encourages faculty to explore AI.

units.why: The opening says AI's benefits should be reaped 'while preserving the intellectual integrity and human-centered model of our university'; an institution-level statement of purpose and principle, so P56 and not a rule for students.
units.anchor: reap its benefits while preserving the intellectual integrity and human-centered model of our university

units.why: Names AI's potential to reshape education and research as a benefit with no rule attached, so P87 rather than P56.
units.anchor: Tulane University recognizes the potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to reshape

units.why: The Institute is described as enhancing data literacy and 'preparing students for future careers'; it is literacy resources for students and staff, closest to P70, though it concerns data literacy not AI literacy.
units.anchor: enhance data literacy across all disciplines, preparing students for future careers
units.fit_note: Concerns data literacy rather than AI literacy specifically, and is an initiative description rather than a mandate.

units.why: Describes new AI centers as showing commitment to leadership in AI research; an institutional investment statement, not a rule, and no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: commitment to being a leader in AI research and application
units.uncovered_note: The university states its investment in AI research centers and its aim of leadership in AI research and application.

units.why: Announces infrastructure investment across research, education management, operations and administration; nearest is P76 (operational AI), but it announces funding rather than rules.
units.anchor: Investments in cross-disciplinary upgrades will support various university operations
units.fit_note: Announces infrastructure investment for operations rather than setting rules for operational AI use.

units.why: Says cross-campus working groups of experts are being assembled to shape guidelines; this describes the body making the policy, so P84.
units.anchor: assembling experts in intellectual property, data privacy, and security

units.why: Describes the provost establishing two AI committees to learn about campus needs; how and by whom guidance is developed, P84.
units.anchor: the provost established two committees to learn more about the current campus environment

units.why: The site defers student AI use to existing academic integrity policies instead of writing new rules; compliance with existing policy, P77. P45 does not fit because no collaborator analogy is drawn.
units.anchor: the major questions about the use of AI by our students are already covered

units.why: Names accuracy, bias and privacy concerns about AI as an institutional concern, not an instruction to verify, so P53 rather than P31.
units.anchor: can raise concerns about accuracy, potential biases, and privacy
units.fit_note: Also names accuracy and privacy, which the type does not centre on.

units.why: Tells students, faculty and staff to consult 'the necessary bodies' before using such tools; checking with institutional bodies for safe use fits P50 (prefer vetted tools) only partly; P10 is about asking the instructor.
units.anchor: students, faculty and staff should consult with the necessary bodies to ensure safe
units.fit_note: Directs consultation with unspecified institutional bodies before use rather than naming vetted tools.

units.why: States a duty on all members to protect university data; data protection, P50.
units.anchor: responsibility to protect university data from unauthorized access or disclosure

units.why: Says Level 2-4 classified data 'should not be entered' into public generative AI tools; protects confidential data, P50 (not P20, which is about assignment specs or student code).
units.anchor: should not be entered into publicly available generative AI tools

units.why: Fact that default-settings inputs are not private; explains why data must be protected, P50.
units.anchor: Information shared with generative AI tools using default settings is not private

units.why: Requires a security and risk review of procured generative AI tools; review of tools before deployment is P65 (broadened).
units.anchor: require a security and risk review by the Tulane Information Security Office

units.why: Directs people to the CISO for questions about AI, data classification and review; it names a contact that supports interpretation of the policy, P80 partly.
units.anchor: please contact
units.fit_note: A help contact rather than an office with enforcement or exception authority.

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to explore AI instead of restricting it; faculty experimentation is P63, though it also signals a permissive attitude.
units.anchor: Rather than restricting AI, faculty are encouraged to explore its potential
units.fit_note: Also signals a non-restrictive institutional attitude toward AI.

units.why: Explains that experimenting helps faculty see which projects AI can handle, a reason to learn AI before setting course policy, P63.
units.anchor: Experimenting with AI can help identify which projects can be effectively handled

units.why: Suggests assignment designs ('requiring students to incorporate personal experiences') that adapt to AI; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: requiring students to incorporate personal experiences, cite sources accurately, or compare diverse ideas

units.why: Asks all community members to actively engage in AI integration; P88 only partly, since that type is about external peers and partners.
units.anchor: should actively engage as we integrate AI into our educational and administrative processes
units.fit_note: Engagement here is internal community participation, not coalitions or external partners.

units.why: Each instructor may set the rule for their course; AI use is decided per instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Each instructor has the option of putting in place guidelines that make the most sense

units.why: Instructors' AI instructions 'must be clear and precise'; a requirement to communicate expectations, closest to P09 though it does not name the syllabus.
units.anchor: instructions must be clear and precise
units.fit_note: Requires clear instructions but does not specify the syllabus as the place.

units.why: Where AI is permitted, students 'should be encouraged' to describe their use; a soft disclosure expectation, P24.
units.anchor: students should be encouraged to describe how AI tools were used
units.fit_note: Phrased as encouragement rather than a mandatory statement.

units.why: Says policies will be revised on an ongoing basis; P54.
units.anchor: on-going efforts to enhance and revise our policies

units.why: Directs instructors with teaching-related AI questions to CELT; support for faculty, P63.
units.anchor: using Artificial Intelligence tools in your teaching or classroom, please contact

units.why: Says the site exists to share the latest AI developments; keeping people informed, P102 partly.
units.anchor: share the latest advancements in AI advancements and implications for the university
units.fit_note: The site offers information rather than imposing a duty to stay informed.

units.why: Commits to workshops for the whole community on AI uses; community-wide training is P70 (not P63, which is faculty-only).
units.anchor: the university will introduce workshops to help the community understand and harness

documents.title: AI Research (Tulane student guidance on AI use)
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'Tulane does not ban AI. Your instructor sets the rules for your course' and tells students to check each syllabus. It sets no single rule and hands the decision to instructors, with unauthorized generative AI covered as a Code of Academic Conduct violation, so delegates.
documents.summary: Library guide restating that Tulane does not ban AI and instructors set course rules. It lays out student responsibilities (ownership, verification, disclosure, data privacy) and a cost-benefit ledger of generative and non-generative AI by research phase.

units.why: States no university-wide ban ('Tulane does not ban AI'), a permissive default, P02; the instructor-decides part is coded separately.
units.anchor: Tulane does not ban AI.
units.fit_note: Says there is no ban rather than welcoming or encouraging use.

units.why: Students are told the instructor sets the course rules, so P04.
units.anchor: Your instructor sets the rules for your course

units.why: Says academic integrity policies apply in full to AI use; compliance with existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: Tulane's academic integrity policies apply in full.

units.why: Directs students ('Check') to read the AI statement in every syllabus each semester; students must find and follow each course's rules, P78 (not P09, which binds instructors).
units.anchor: Check the AI statement in every syllabus, every semester.

units.why: Defines AI to set what the guidance covers, P61.
units.anchor: Artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems that perform tasks

units.why: Defines generative AI as creating 'new text, images, summaries, or citations', distinguishing it from non-generative AI so the guidance can say how to use each: P61.
units.anchor: Creates new text, images, summaries, or citations by predicting likely patterns

units.why: Warns generative output looks plausible but may be inaccurate; the output-reliability type is P31.
units.anchor: Output is plausible-sounding, which is not the same as accurate.
units.fit_note: A caution about the tool rather than an explicit instruction to verify (given elsewhere).

units.why: Defines non-generative AI-assisted tools to separate them from generative AI; definition, P61.
units.anchor: Searches, sorts, filters, and organizes information that already exists, without inventing new content.

units.why: Notes non-generative tools have a lighter environmental footprint; environmental concern, P53.
units.anchor: Generally a lighter environmental footprint.

units.why: Students are sole authors and 'fully responsible' for AI content they incorporate; P29.
units.anchor: you are therefore fully responsible for any AI-generated content you incorporate into assignments

units.why: Unauthorized assistance including generative AI used to write or rewrite significant work is a Code of Academic Conduct violation; classifies misuse as misconduct, P36 (the best single home, though P19 also applies).
units.anchor: including generative AI to write or rewrite significant elements of your work, is a violation
units.fit_note: Also forbids generative AI writing or rewriting significant elements of one's work unless authorized.

units.why: States AI can invent sources and err; supports the duty to verify, P31.
units.anchor: AI tools can invent sources, produce biased summaries, and make factual errors.

units.why: Students must fact-check and critically evaluate AI output before submitting; P31.
units.anchor: solely responsible for fact-checking and critically evaluating all AI-generated output

units.why: Where permitted, students should describe their AI use, with an example; disclosure statement, P24.
units.anchor: where AI use is permitted, you should describe how you used it

units.why: Failure to disclose is itself a possible violation; P28.
units.anchor: Failure to disclose when disclosure is expected is a breach of transparency

units.why: Students should not enter Level 2-4 data into public generative AI tools; data protection, P50.
units.anchor: should not be entered into publicly available generative AI tools

units.why: Explains default-setting inputs are not private; P50.
units.anchor: Information shared with generative AI using default settings is not private

units.why: Tells students to read the tradeoffs 'as a ledger rather than a ban list' and weigh gains and costs per task; no type captures a weigh-costs-and-benefits stance, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Read them as a ledger rather than a ban list
units.uncovered_note: Students are told to weigh the gains and costs of AI at each research phase rather than follow a default or a ban.

units.why: Lists topic suggestions as a gain of generative AI at the topic-choice phase; a benefit statement, P87 (not P15, since it is presented as a gain, not a permitted use).
units.anchor: Topic suggestions in seconds

units.why: Lists quick summaries as a gain of generative AI when assessing sources; benefit, P87.
units.anchor: Summaries in seconds

units.why: Names the environmental cost of each generative AI prompt: P53.
units.anchor: Energy and water consumed on every prompt

units.why: Warns AI-suggested topics are less original; no exact type, P31 (limits of AI output) is nearest.
units.anchor: Topics are less original, constrained by model training
units.fit_note: Concerns originality rather than correctness of output.

units.why: Warns of fabricated citations that require verifying every result; P31.
units.anchor: Fabricated citations mean verifying every single result

units.why: Says AI summaries do not build skills that reading builds; AI shortcuts skill-building practice, P41.
units.anchor: Does not help build the mental models and critical thinking skills that reading builds

units.why: Reliance on AI summaries weakens synthesis and evaluation skills; P41.
units.anchor: Reliance on AI summaries weakens synthesis capacity and critical evaluation

units.why: Warns that uploading licensed content may violate terms; licensing and terms of use, P52 (P49 would be a prohibition, which this cost entry only implies).
units.anchor: Uploading licensed content may violate terms and retain your data

units.why: Warns uploading library content may breach policies or publisher terms and risk campus-wide access loss; P52 terms of use.
units.anchor: put the university at risk of campus-wide access termination

units.why: Instruction to verify every citation ('Verify'), P31.
units.anchor: Verify every citation against the actual source; fabrication is common.

units.why: Tells students to assume inputs may train models; privacy awareness, P50.
units.anchor: Assume your inputs may be used to train future models.

units.why: Prohibits pasting licensed, confidential or unpublished content into consumer AI tools; protected works, P49.
units.anchor: Do not paste licensed, confidential, or unpublished content into consumer AI tools.

units.why: Tells students to disclose AI use to instructors, editors or reviewers; P24.
units.anchor: Disclose your use to instructors, editors, or reviewers.

units.why: Asks students to account for the gaps that come from depending on AI; the learning-cost warning P41 fits best.
units.anchor: Account for the intellectual gaps that come from depending on AI-generated content.
units.fit_note: An instruction to account for gaps rather than a claim that AI shortcuts practice.

units.why: Tells students to use licensed content only inside the database's own AI interface; approved-tool use, P92 (not P17, which is course-specific).
units.anchor: use licensed library content only inside its native database's AI interface
units.fit_note: Concerns the vendor's native AI interface for licensed content, not a university-wide approved list.

units.why: A fact about AI limits; P31 is nearest as it concerns reliability of AI output.
units.anchor: AI cannot reach resources behind paywalls or subscription databases.
units.fit_note: A coverage limitation rather than wrong or hallucinated output.

units.why: Where the instructor permits AI, students must acknowledge it; P24.
units.anchor: If your instructor permits AI use, you must acknowledge it.

units.why: Students are told to ask the instructor for the citation style; closest is P10 (ask before), though it concerns style, not whether use is allowed.
units.anchor: Consult your instructor for their preferred style.
units.fit_note: Asks the instructor about citation style, not whether a use is allowed.

units.why: Says most AI-using assignments need both a citation of specific output and a disclosure statement; P25 chosen since it distinguishes what a citation contains.
units.anchor: most assignments that use AI need both
units.fit_note: Distinguishes citation from disclosure without listing tool, prompt, or date.

notes: Only two university-layer documents included; the Provost's letter was not available. The library guide is a secondary source from an education library guide, so its scope is wider than computing.
